rationale: Receipt 8c866b71bf0e470e900a15e895b2bed9 (completed, exit 0, TestAssuranceRestoreCommittedLogsContext passed, 55 parsed events) exercised the applied-state phase added to the healed partition, and it records the state-machine-level form of the divergence the account previously held only for log stores. I register that as a new fact and rewrite the question-level account around it, dropping the limitation that the two state machines were unexercised. Six comparisons were evaluated: leadership convergence after healing and the flag-disabled control hold; the surviving-entry predicate and the new applied-divergence predicate are violated; the continuation predicate (a client entry applied after healing reaches both peers' FSMs) holds, which is what rules out a stalled cluster. No counterevidence was found for the new consequence, and the earlier counterevidence and the remaining limits carry over with the state-machine limitation replaced.

knowledge.statement: In the retained healed-partition applied-state execution two state machines held different committed values for the same log index while the cluster kept serving clients: with the flag enabled the restarted side's store and the first peer's store still disagreed at log index 118 after healing - the restarted side held a LogConfiguration entry there and the peer a LogCommand entry - both sides had applied through index 121 (restarted side applied 121, the minimum applied position of the two peers 121; the first side's own payload at 119, the second side's at 118), and a client entry applied after healing committed at index 121 and was applied by the restarted instance and by both peers (post_heal_payload_on_first_side_fsm 1, post_heal_payload_on_second_side_fsm 2, heal_leader_present true), so ordinary replication after healing carried the cluster forward over the conflict without reconciling it. With the flag disabled the same measurement reported no disagreeing index (conflict_index 0), applied positions of 119 on both sides and the single committed entry.
knowledge.conditions: Three-voter committed configuration recorded at log index 106 while the restarted node's snapshot metadata carries a single-voter configuration; the partition case's conditions, in which the restarted side leads on its reconstruction with a fresh instance beside it while the two peers of the committed configuration lead on their own, both sides committing a uniquely named entry in the same term; the connections are then restored in both directions and one further client entry is applied with a 1500 ms timeout by whichever instance is in Leader state, after which the case compares the two stores over their shared range, reads both sides' applied positions and searches each instance's FSM for the payloads. The healed leader in this receipt was the peer side (first_side_state Follower, first_side_term 4), and the observation window is 1600 ms of healing plus 800 ms after the new commit.

interpretations.rationale: The configuration a restarted node uses for elections and for counting committed support is not the committed configuration recorded in its own log whenever the tracked commit index covers that node's last configuration entry, and the consequences of that context are now exercised through to the applied state of the instances. The mechanism: restoreFromCommittedLogs reads the tracked commit index, sets the commit index and applies the committed prefix to the FSM, advancing lastApplied [restore_lastapplied], and NewRaft's configuration scan then re-derives configurations only for configuration entries above max(lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied) [scan_start, cfg_entry], so a committed configuration entry inside that prefix is never re-derived and the node keeps whatever snapshot metadata installed, or nothing at all. Receipts record the divergence in both directions across five restart shapes [4d96d7967e324d6a98cfef381c9cad6a-knowledge-1]. Receipt 8c866b71bf0e470e900a15e895b2bed9 carries the applied-state phase: after the partition was healed, one client entry committed at index 121 and was applied by the restarted instance and by both peers, while the restarted side's store kept a LogConfiguration entry at index 118 and the peer's a LogCommand entry there, and both sides had applied through 121 - so the two state machines hold different values for log index 118 while the cluster keeps committing to all of them. That is the same-object, before-and-after confirmation the mechanism needs: both sides applied their own store's entry at that index [apply_own_log], the two entries agree in the term that decides whether AppendEntries treats them as duplicates [append_new], and each new leader's no-op wrote at the same index on both sides, which is how the conflict came to sit under a matching term in the first place [leader_noop]. The remaining consequences each stand on their own receipts: bounded non-progress, leadership and commits resting on a minority of the committed configuration, a client-acknowledged commit resting on one copy or discarded from every store, votes granted and recorded for a node without a vote, a non-voting peer that campaigned and became Leader, a client membership change that replaces the committed configuration with support that is not its majority, two leaders in one term under a partition, and the two divergent committed histories that survive healing. What the receipts still do not establish is how an application would detect the divergence, or what the two FSMs hold for entries applied through a snapshot transfer.
counterevidence: The feature's documented purpose is replaying known-committed logs into the FSM; nothing in the sources makes skipping committed configuration entries a required behaviour, and the existing TestRaft_RestoreCommittedLogs asserts only applied index, tracked commit index and log indices, so it neither exercises nor contradicts the configuration reconstruction.

Competing explanation that the flag's committed-log replay itself, rather than the skipped configuration entry, produces these effects: excluded wherever tested, by the within-flag case whose configuration entry lies above the replayed prefix and by the flag-disabled controls in every receipt, which hold the published configuration and refuse the same requests, decisions, changes and leadership - including the control in receipt 8c866b71bf0e470e900a15e895b2bed9, where the same applied-state measurement reports no disagreeing index.

Each consequence needs its stated conditions, and the applied-state observation is a consequence of the conditions being met earlier: the partition must have produced two leaders in one term, which in turn needs the two sides physically separated and the restarted side able to reach a quorum of its own reconstruction.

The healed and applied-state windows together are 2400 ms and observe log stores, applied positions and the MockFSM's applied payloads only; a later snapshot transfer, a further election, an application-level reconciliation or an operator action could still change the end state, and none of those paths was exercised.
limitations: Single process with in-memory transports and in-memory commit-tracking stores, no crash injection, no disk-backed store and no network fault model beyond the transport's own Disconnect and Connect.

Single-shot windows (200-1600 ms depending on the case, 3000 ms for leadership, 1000-1500 ms for commits) and one or two restarted instances per case; the partition outcome is reproduced twice and the applied divergence is now observed once after healing, but no rate, longer-run or long-stability claim follows.

The applied state is read as the payloads each MockFSM has applied plus each instance's applied position; entries delivered through a snapshot transfer, application-level detection or repair, and a snapshot taken after healing are unexercised.

The reconstruction shapes beyond the five exercised ladders, other stores and other configuration flags were not varied; the LogCache entries record a separate startup-plumbing gap rather than a consensus consequence.
